newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: India's neighbours welcome Gujral's appointment.
newsitem.headline: India's neighbours welcome Gujral's appointment.

text.p: India's neighbours on Monday welcomed the appointment of Inder Kumar Gujral as prime minister, saying he would help smooth regional tensions.
Pakistani newspapers said Gujral would pursue a policy he crafted as foreign minister under the previous government of seeking better ties with India's old rival Pakistan and its other neighbours.

"One of the best things about his becoming India's next prime minister is that the process of normalisation of ties between India and Pakistan will move ahead," said the Islamabad-based English-language newspaper The News.

"In India, with the selection of I.K. Gujral as prime minister, stability is expected to return to the world's largest democracy," the paper said. "Such a development is conducive to reducing tensions in the region."
Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif's media adviser Mushahid Hussain said on Sunday that Pakistan welcomed Gujral as prime minister.

"We...hope that Mr Gujral, as he was stating when he was not in the government in the past, would take steps to resolve the primary cause of friction between India and Pakistan, namely the the unresolved dispute of Jammu and Kashmir," Hussain said.
India and Pakistan have fought three wars since independence from Britain 50 years ago, two of them over Kashmir.
Top Pakistani and Indian diplomats met for three days in New Delhi at the end of March, the first such talks since 1994.
Gujral, as foreign minister, met his Pakistani counterpart Gohar Ayub Khan in Delhi this month and is now likely to meet Sharif at a regional summit meeting in the Maldives in May.
Chinese Premier Li Peng congratulated Gujral and voiced hope Sino-Indian ties would improve further.

"It is the common aspiration of the two governments and two peoples to build Sino-Indian future-oriented constructive and cooperative partnership," Xinhua news agency quoted Li as saying in the congratulatory message to Gujral.
Beijing and Delhi fought a brief war over sections of their 4,000 kilometre (2,500 mile) border in 1962, but tensions between the two Asian giants have eased after years of talks.
Bangladesh's Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina sent a warmly worded message of congratulations to Gujral.

"We regard you as a genuine friend of Bangladesh and hold you in high esteem for your personal interest in and valuable contribution to promotion and strengthening of Bangladesh-India friendship and cooperation," her message said.
She said Gujral's initiatives had led to "significant developments" in bilateral relations in recent months.

During the 10-month rule of former Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda, Bangladesh and India signed a landmark 30-year river sharing treaty and reached agreements to repatriate Bangladeshi tribal refugees from India and jointly fight insurgencies.
Sri Lanka said Gujral was an old friend who had worked hard to improve bilateral ties.
"... there could be no more fitting choice to lead India in this, its 50th anniversary year of independence," President Chandrika Kumaratunga said in a message to Gujral.
Foreign Minister Lakshman Kadirgamar said he believed that under Gujral's leadership ties between the two countries "will enter a period of unparalleled strength and mutual benefit."
Sri Lanka's ties with India touched a low in the late 1980s after Indian troops arrived to disarm Tamil rebels under a controversial agreement between the two countries.
The troops left in 1990 after suffering heavy casualties and failing to defeat the rebels. Gujral was then foreign minister.
Sri Lankan newspapers said Gujral would be able to reduce regional tension by forging closer ties with Pakistan and China.
The Observer said Gujral was a firm believer in defusing tensions with neighbours and "nurturing trust and confidence".

Gujral said in Colombo in January that India was ready to do anything to help bring the island's 13-year-old ethnic conflict to an end. He also promised to lift trade barriers to help increase Sri Lankan exports to its huge neighbour.
